newsitem.title: USA: American pilots' union cautiously optimistic on vote.
newsitem.headline: American pilots' union cautiously optimistic on vote.

text.p: Leaders of the American Airlines pilots union endorsed a tentative labour agreement with the carrier on Friday and expressed optimism that the rank-and-file would approve the deal.
The leaders of the Allied Pilots Association said they would ask their 9,300 members who work for American to vote on the proposal within six weeks.
Last fall APA members defied their leadership and voted to reject a proposed contract despite the union board's recommendation for approval.

The pilots, who briefly struck the airline in February before President Clinton ordered them back to work, could strike within 30 days if they reject the latest offer from the airline, a unit of Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp.
On Wall Street, investors applauded the lastest news by boosting AMR's stock $3.875 to $86.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The union's 18-member board voted 12 to six to begin a process by which union members are expected to cast ballots within the next six weeks.

"I think the board's vote is reflective of the membership," said Brian Mayhew, chairman of the Allied Pilots Association board's negotiating committee. "I would expect (the proposal) to be approved by something like the margin of the board of directors' vote," he said.
The board spent two days at a suburban Chicago hotel discussing the contract proposal, reached March 19.
American Airlines welcomed the acceptance of the propsoal by the union as a signal the labour dispute may be nearing an end.
"The tentative agreement reflects compromise and creativity from both sides," airline President Donald Carty said in a statement.
The issue of who will fly smaller jets at American Airlines' regional carrier, American Eagle, was the major concern of most pilots, union officials said.
American Airlines wants American Eagle pilots, who are paid less than APA members, to fly smaller jets so the company can remain competitive with low-cost commuter carriers.
The APA pilots are concerned that American Eagle pilots will eventually take over their current routes.

The proposed five-year agreement includes a 9 percent wage increase, 5.75 million stock options and a guarantee that furloughed pilots will be able to fly new jets that the carrier is buying for American Eagle.
APA President James Sovich said the union will hold a series of meetings with pilots in nine U.S. cities over the next two weeks aimed at explaining terms of the proposal.
Although he declined to speculate on how the rank-and-file would vote, Sovich said the union board's position has not changed in recent weeks.
"Our position is the same as it was 10 days ago. There is no more to be gained by more negotiations," Sovich told a news conference.
Sovich said the pilots could still launch a second strike by rejecting the latest agreement because they feel their concerns over the smaller jets have not been addressed.

"If the membership is willing to strike over the regional jet issue, we will strike (against American Airlines)," Sovich said. "These are educated adults. We'll just present them with the information in the contract."
